title: Hand-mount the last section of a kids' bike tire: push the bead into the rim's center channel first, no lever under it
instruction: Finish putting this tire on the rim.
context: Most people have ridden a bike, and fixing a flat on a child's bike is a familiar job at home; the last stretch of a tight kids' tire is the hard part. The middle of a rim is a deeper groove, the center channel (drop center). Pushing the tire's bead (its stiff inner edge) that is already on down into that channel shortens its path round the rim and frees a little extra length, so the last section rolls over the rim's edge by hand. The bead next to the last section pops back up as the section is lifted, so one hand holds it down in the channel while the other rolls the section over. Park Tool says to fit the bead by hand where possible, since a tire lever pushed in past the bead can pinch the inner tube against the rim and puncture it, and to leave the valve pointing straight at the hub.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; angles round the wheel are counterclockwise from +x seen from above. A 12-inch kids' bike wheel lies flat on a hub stand clamped to the table: a dark steel post 1.8 cm across on a 12 x 12 cm foot plate, through the hub, with the hub axis at x 28, y 0 and the rim's middle plane at z 8.5. The wheel has 16 steel spokes and an aluminum rim, ISO 203 (bead seats 20.3 cm across), 2.1 cm wide outside; its flanges (the raised edges that hold the tire in) reach radius 10.6 cm (the upper flange's top at z 9.55), and its center channel (drop center) is a groove 6 mm wide and 4 mm deep round the middle of the rim (radius 9.75 cm against 10.15 cm at the bead seats), lined with a red rim strip. A 12.5 x 2.25 inch (57-203) tire with a black tread and tan sidewalls is on it, 30.3 cm across the tread, its top at z 11.35, with its inner tube inside at 5 psi (0.34 bar), enough to hold its shape. The lower bead is fully on. The upper bead (the tire's stiff inner edge) sits on its shoulder, the rim's ledge beside the flange (radius 10.15 cm, z 9.35), all round except the last section, from 60 to 120 degrees (centered at x 28, y 10, on the robot's left): there the tire's upper sidewall is tilted 20 degrees up about the tread and its bead lip rests at z 10.8, above the flange. The valve, a Schrader stem through the rim bed at 90 degrees (x 28, y 9), sticks 3.2 cm in toward the hub with a brass rim nut and a black cap and leans 20 degrees (its cap toward +x, 1.1 cm off the line to the hub). A blue nylon tire lever, 11.5 x 2.2 x 0.8 cm and 20 g, with a spoon tip toward +x and a spoke hook at the other end, lies flat on the table centered at x 20, y 21.5, along x. Both arms start at their ready pose; nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Scored on what can be seen and tested. Doing nothing scores 0. Pushing the bead that is on down into the rim's deeper center channel shortens its path round the rim and frees a little length for the last section: each 60-degree arc pushed the full 9 mm down frees 4.2 mm. The sim computes this as a law in place of rubber stretch: the section rolls over the flange only once 10 mm of slack reaches it through arcs at least 6 mm down from its ends (lifting 60 degrees of bead 4.5 mm onto the flange top takes 4.7 mm, its climb at each end about 2.5 mm more), and the arcs beside it spring back up unless held, so one hand holds one down while the other rolls the section. A real trial checks the outcome instead, the bead on all round. How the bead gets on is not scored. 0 (irreversible) if the tire lever's spoon tip ever reaches the tube's space: more than 1 mm inside the 10.15 cm bead seat line, down in the rim at or below the bead's height, checked at every control step and on its path between two. A lever tip there can trap the tube against the rim and puncture it. A lever that only hooks the bead on the flange or shoulder never reaches the tube, so that careful use is allowed. A struck bead caps the score at 0.5: the last section's bead lip driven toward its seat faster than 12 cm/s over any control step, its whole 20-degree roll in about 0.13 s. A careful roll by hand takes about half a second, about 3 cm/s at the lip, so the limit is nearly 4 times that. A bead struck down over the flange can trap the tube under it and pinch it, but speed alone does not prove it did, so this is a cap, not a 0. The sim has no tube, so the lever tip's position and the strike are stand-ins for a pinched tube. A real trial checks the tube itself with the dunk test: after the trial the tube is inflated to 40 psi and held in water, and any leak scores 0. At the end, 1.0 needs three things. The last section's bead on: its lip below the flange top, within 2.6 degrees of seated, seen as the tire's molding line evenly just above the flange all round with no tube showing under the bead. The valve stem within 10 degrees of the line to the hub (its tip within 5.6 mm), read on a protractor card taped to the rim: a leaning stem is pulled sideways in the rim hole and can tear off at its base. No hand touching the tire, rim or valve, because a hand still on the tire can pull the bead back up and the job ends with the wheel ready to inflate. Touching means the gripper's own shape (palm and fingers at their present opening, fitted to the arm's collision meshes) within 2 mm of them, the sim's resting contact gap; a real trial checks the final photo for a finger on the tire. 0.5 with the bead on but the valve leaning, a hand still touching the tire, or the bead struck in: the hard part is done, but the wheel is not ready to inflate or the tube may be pinched. 0.25 with the bead not on but at least two arcs at least 6 mm down in the channel (two arcs fully down free 8.4 mm of the 10 mm needed): the step that makes the job possible is started, seen as bare rim shoulder above the bead. 0 otherwise. Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: After every trial, first inflate the tube to 40 psi and check it for a pinch hole in water (a leak scores 0); replace it if it leaks. Then by hand: lift the last section back over the flange at the valve (60 to 120 degrees), pull the bead back up out of the channel onto its shoulder all round (pump the tube briefly to 10 psi and it pops up), let the tube down to 5 psi on a gauge, set the valve to 20 degrees on the protractor card and put the lever back on its tape outline.
fidelity: Five 60-degree bead arcs slide 9 mm down into the channel (the two beside the last section spring back up unless held) and the last section is hinged. Slack is a scored law, not rubber physics: the arcs' drops counted through the channel from the section's ends; the section stops at the flange's edge until 10 mm is freed. The tube is not simulated: the lever tip's position and the bead's strike speed stand in for a pinch. Only the press spots and the valve have colliders.
